extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, copyholders, and printers (publishing professionals)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and style rules for preparing manuscripts and for proofreading/page make-up in book and periodical publishing, including manuscript handling, pagination, proofs, headings, indentation, punctuation, and proofreader marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing in American and English sums of money
rubrics_metrics.description: In American and English sums of money no space is used between the symbols, $, and £ (pounds), s. (shillings), and d. (pence), and the numerals (an en leader is used for a decimal point): $2,375; £10 38. 2d; 107.0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use no space between currency symbols and numerals; use an en leader for decimal point where shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quads after numerals at line beginnings
rubrics_metrics.description: After Arabic and Roman numerals at the beginning of lines, denoting subsections, there should be an en quad. After Arabic and Roman numerals at the beginning of center-heads there should be an em quad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use en quad for subsection-line numerals; em quad for numerals at beginning of center-heads; follow different quad spacing for small-cap and cap headings (small-cap: en quad between words; cap-and-small-cap and cap headings: two 3-em spaces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation by measure and type size (plain paragraphs)
rubrics_metrics.description: In measures of less than 10 picas’ width, indent all sizes 1 em. In measures of from 10 to 20, indent 11-pt., rem; 10-pt., 14; 9-pt., 14; 8-pt., 14; 6-pt., 2. In measures of from 20 to 30, indent 11-pt.,14 ems; 10-pt., 14; 9-pt., 14; 8-pt., 2; 6-pt., 24. This is for plain paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply specified first-line indents depending on measure (column width) and type size for plain paragraphs; follow table precisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation by measure and type size (hanging paragraphs)
rubrics_metrics.description: In hanging indentions, in measures of less than 10 picas, indent all sizes 1 em; from 10 to 20, 11-pt., 10-pt., 9-pt., and 8-pt., 13 ems; 6-pt., 2 ems; from 20 to 30, 11-pt., 10-pt., 9-pt., and 8-pt., 2 ems; 6-pt., 3 ems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the listed hanging-indent values according to measure and type size when setting hanging paragraphs (first line flush, others indented).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry centering and indentation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry, center the longest line and let the indention be governed by that; if the longest line is disproportionate, strike an average of the long lines. Where quotations from different poems vary slightly in length, indent all alike. Indent according to rhymes and length of lines. In blank verse, align lines approximately the same length; align consecutive rhyming lines or indent alternating rhymes alike; disproportionately short lines should be indented more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center by longest (or average) long line; align or indent based on rhyme patterns and line length to give a centered appearance; follow examples for rhyming schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for plain paragraphs and use of hanging indention
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter “plain paragraphs” are always preferable. Where it is desired to bring into relief the opening word or words of a paragraph, or the number introducing such paragraph, or where a center-head makes more than three lines, “hanging indention” is often employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default to plain paragraphs; use hanging indention sparingly to emphasize openings, numbers, or long center-heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leads, slugs, and leadded vs solid setting
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead is a strip of metal used to separate lines of type; the ordinary lead is 2 points thick. Matter with leads between the lines is called leaded; without, solid. A slug is thicker than a lead, used after headlines; standard sizes are 6 and 12 points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and apply lead/slug conventions when specifying interline spacing and page make-up; most books are leaded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center-heads, side-heads, cut-in heads: definitions and treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: A center-head is a headline placed at equal distances from both margins, usually set in caps or small caps. A side-head is a headline placed at the side of the page/column, often set in italics with only the first word and proper names capitalized; may be set flush or run in. A cut-in head is placed in a box cut into the side of the type-page and usually set in different type under the first two lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose head type appropriate to structure and length; for multi-line center-heads use pyramid form (2–3 lines) or hanging indention (more than 3 lines); follow capitalization and font recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running-head rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A running-head is a headline placed at the top of each page, usually giving the main title on the left-hand (verso) page and chapter title on the right (recto). A good working-rule is to set them in roman or italic capitals two sizes (points) smaller than the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep running-heads consistent and two sizes smaller than body text; use appropriate content on verso/recto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of plain vs hanging paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: A plain (or regular) paragraph has the first line indented and the others set flush. A hanging paragraph has the first line set flush and the others indented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply correct indentation style depending on paragraph type; use hanging for lists, long headings, etc., as instructed elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of proofs and their meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Galley-proof: impression of type in a galley; page-proof: impression of type made up into page form; plate- or foundry-proof: proof taken before an electrotype cast (has black border); foul proof: galley-proof containing author's corrections; revise: a new proof corrected from a marked proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct proof types at correct stages; understand that plate corrections are expensive and likely to injure plates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make-up definition and folio conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Make-up is arranging into page-form of type-lines. A folio is a page-number (even on verso, odd on recto). A drop-folio is a page-number placed at the bottom of a page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow folio conventions when paginating; designate drop-folio when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Half-title (bastard title) and title-page copy submission
rubrics_metrics.description: A half-title or bastard title is the abbreviated title on a separate page preceding the full title-page. Copy for title-pages, prefaces, tables of contents, etc., should be submitted with the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide all front-matter copy with manuscript to avoid delays; index copy should be compiled from special page-proofs and delivered promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting machine notes (monotype/linotype) and reset implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Linotype and monotype processes differ in resetting behavior: in linotype the slightest change necessitates resetting the whole line (and this affects footnote numbering), while in monotype or hand-set matter substitution of a number is simpler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number footnotes consecutively through article/chapters to minimize linotype resetting problems; be aware that mid-stream numbering changes can force widespread resetting and cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript preparation: legibility, size, and handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should be typewritten or in perfectly clear handwriting (typewritten preferable). Sheets should be uniform size (9x11" desirable). Use only one side of paper. Never roll manuscripts; place them flat in a box or an envelope. Do not fasten except by pins or clips; when fastening pieces together use mucilage not pins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow handling and submission rules precisely to avoid loss/damage and to make compositor's job easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Margins, pagination, and inserts marking
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave liberal margins at top and left for reader/printer directions. Pages should be numbered consecutively. Inserted pages should be clearly indicated (e.g., '4A', '4B'); omitted pages indicated (e.g., number p. 4, '4-7'). Additions placed after sheets to which they belong and marked 'Insert A', etc., with insertion point indicated in margin ('Here insert A').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear marking of inserts/omissions prevents misplacement and pagination errors; maintain uniform sheets and margins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph indication in manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraphs should be plainly indicated, either by indenting the first line or by a § mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure paragraph breaks are unambiguous in manuscript to ease typesetting and proofing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote designation and numbering
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes should be clearly designated, separated from the text (e.g., by a rule) or by using ink of different color. The word in the text carrying the note should be followed by a superior figure corresponding to that preceding the note. Footnotes should never be run into the text in manuscripts (whether in parentheses or otherwise). Number them consecutively throughout an article or by chapters in a book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid per-page numbering when setting by linotype; consecutive numbering reduces resetting and confusion. Use superior figures and clear separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-reading: promptness, standard marks, and answering queries
rubrics_metrics.description: Read and return your proofs promptly. In marking proof-sheets use the standard proofreaders’ marks (see p. 123). Do not adopt a system of your own. Be careful to answer all queries in the proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely and standardized corrections reduce delays and errors; unanswered queries cause mistakes and extra cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize changes and beware of cost of alterations
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember that changes in the type cost money. The omission or addition of a word in the middle of a paragraph may necessitate resetting the whole of this from that point on; each succeeding stage will add to the cost. Corrections in plates should be studiously avoided — expensive and likely to injure plates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make manuscripts as perfect as possible before delivery; limit late changes to reduce cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return and documentation with successive proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The original manuscript should be returned with the galley-proof, so the proofreader may refer to it; each successive set of proofs returned should be accompanied by the previous marked set. This assists in calculating costs of alterations properly chargeable to the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always include originals and prior marked proofs to maintain a clear record and proper charge accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hints to proofreaders — core responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Read everything as if you yourself were the author. Be particularly careful about proper names and figures. If the copy is not clear, look it up or query the author. Make your queries clear and transfer manuscript queries to the proof. Be discreet; avoid trivial criticisms. Correct anything palpably wrong; you are the judge. Do not follow copy blindly; follow copy only when correct. Do not ask authors/editors to decide style questions — the Manual of Style is primarily meant for you. Cultivate speed but value accuracy over dispatch. In unavoidable rush, protect yourself by stating limits of responsibility. Put your initial at the top of every galley you read or revise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofreaders have primary responsibility for typographical requirements and adopted style; exercise judgment, preserve accuracy, and document work. Initial galleys to track work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hints to copyholders (reading aloud) — conduct and technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate a low, soft, clear reading-voice. Small words are as essential as big ones — get them all in. Enunciate plural 's's distinctly. Do not get offended when asked to repeat. Regulate speed, do not guess at a word, sit at right angles to your reader, give your reader a chance to make corrections, slow up when they put pencil to paper. Evolve a system of signals (e.g., taps) so you don't say 'in italics' for every word. Do not waste time over matters of style; the proofreader knows the rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copyholders should facilitate efficient, accurate proofreading by clear, measured reading and a private signal system; avoid style questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofroom housekeeping and sending proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: In sending out proofs, see that everything is there. Arrange copy and proof-sheets neatly and consecutively. Never send out proofs without consulting the job ticket for number wanted and recipient. The manuscript should accompany the galley-proof; the foul proof should accompany the page-proof; indicate envelope contents at lower left. Fasten pins in center at top, not diagonally over directions. Return reference volumes each evening and keep records/files neat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain neat, orderly proofroom practices to avoid lost items and misdirected proofs; clearly label envelopes and follow sending procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and meaning of standard proofreader’s marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard marks and their meanings are listed (examples: Dele — delete; Letter reversed — turn; Put in place; Close up — no space; Bad spacing — space more evenly; Wrong font; Transpose; Make a new paragraph; Indent; Carry left/right; Elevate; Depress; Imperfect type — correct; Space shows between words — push down; Straighten crooked line; Print ligature; Words are omitted; Query to author; Put in capitals; Put in SMALL-CAPITALS; Put in LOWER-CASE; Put in emer type; Put in italics; Put in bold-face type).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these standardized marks on proofs to communicate corrections unambiguously to compositors and authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headings, titles, and quotation styling (high-level rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of books, essays, cycles of poems, and divisions should have principal words capitalized and be roman-quoted (italicized) as appropriate; center-heads and box-heads use capitals per rules. Documents and chapters follow capitalization and roman-quoting conventions. 'Continued' after headlines set in italics; at end of articles placed in brackets and reduced type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the Manual’s cross-referenced rules for capitalization and roman/italic treatment of different classes of titles and running headlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation and typographic conventions (selected high-level items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comprehensive rules exist for comma usage (141–62) including omission and placement in numerous clause types; use of colon (131–36) for introductions, separation, and scripture clauses; dashes (166–75) for breaks, emphasis, summarizing clauses and connections; ellipses (180–81) rules for omissions and quotations; en dash vs em dash usage; spacing and alignment rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the specified punctuation rules contextually (commas, colons, dashes, ellipses, en/em dashes) as laid out in the Manual; consult relevant sections for edge cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization rules (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive rules for capitalization: proper nouns, adjectives derived from proper nouns, geographic names, books of the Bible, organizations, titles, academic degrees, historical/geological epochs, political bodies, religious denominations, and many other categories; rules and word lists spanning sections 1–57.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the Manual's detailed categories and word lists for capitalization decisions; consult specific section numbers for particular classes (e.g., degrees 21–22, books of the Bible 31, organizations 11–12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of words, hyphenation, and compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for division of words (215–31): avoid unnecessary division; systems of division, use of hyphen to indicate division; compound words—rules for hyphenation, omission of common elements, treatment of prefixes/suffixes (co-, non-, semi-, vice-, ex-, over/under, etc.), and capitalization within compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the prescribed hyphenation rules and compound constructions; prefer avoiding divisions at certain positions (e.g., two-letter splits) and follow etymological or English-system cautions as directed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerals, dates, and figures formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for spelling out centuries and decades, date punctuation and comma use between month and year, use of commas for thousands, column spacing for figures, en dash use instead of comma between consecutive pages in references, and handling of hours/minutes (colon), among others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format numbers and dates according to the Manual’s prescriptions to ensure consistency (e.g., hundreds repeated rules, commas with thousands, spell out certain ranges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliographic and literary references conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for literary references, reduction and punctuation of citations, setting of author names in references, use of en dash/ranges for pages, and treatment of consecutive authors/works. 'Continued' in references set in italics when appropriate; classical references punctuation specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare bibliographies and citations per the Manual's rules for consistency in punctuation, abbreviation, and page-range notation.
